doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Learning new songs and transposing on the spot
summary: A sax player stumps Pallo with a song; he explains thinking in numbers to change keys.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yes. And you, again, like I said, you never stop learning. I used a sax player with me Wednesday night and I asked, it was Nicki Parrott’s sister, she plays alto. And I used her on a gig and she — I said, “Do something in a rumba tempo” and she did it. It was a song I never heard in my life and I forgot the title of it now but I’m going to call her up. Of course I could hear the changes and I just backed her up. But I said, “I never heard that song before.” And she said, “Oh you never heard it? Wow.” It was unbelievable for me not to hear it, especially, you know, I know almost every song from the 1940s up. And she got me. So I’m going to look that song up.
If someone said, “Let’s do ‘Misty,’ let’s do it in B.”
How do you think that? How do you —

Uh, and I’m not going by frets. Let’s say if you’re playing something right here on here, and someone’s going up a full step you just go here. I am not thinking that. Maybe years ago I did, but now I’m thinking of the one four five and so forth and I use the system of knowing the change that’s coming. In other words if I’m in the key of C and you’re going to bring it to say F, I go a fourth up, a fourth up from there and then I know the change. Or I picture it in the key that I do know it in and I know that I’m going to the five change or to the two minor seven change, it’s all there already. It’s like a photograph in there or something.

But there are times you can get stuck, because if there are a mess of changes then you say all right well let me just pick out the main ones and you skip one or something in between. But otherwise no problem. But I never do the where you could just cheat, we call it — it’s not really cheating, it’s like when you put a capo on a guitar. All these people have capos, they’re playing the same chord over and over but they’re in a different key. Same as Irving Berlin we were talking about with the piano. But, so I just could never do that. I’d rather just change to the key you’re supposed to be in. But it’s interesting when someone does change a key. It keeps you on your toes.
Like the women singers are often a fourth or fifth away from where you normally would play it.
